newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Relatives of Cyprus missing cautious on deal.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of Cyprus missing cautious on deal.

text.p: Relatives of missing Cypriots reacted with caution on Friday to news that the leaders of Cyprus's Greek and Turkish communities reached an agreement that could lead to the opening of mass graves of persons listed as missing in hostilities between the two sides.

"We don't just want black bags full of remains... What we want to avoid is going through mass graves ignoring some basic procedures. The rights of the missing persons and the rights of relatives must be respected," said Nick Theodossiou, chairman of the committee of relatives of missing Greek Cypriots.
Under terms of the deal, the two sides will exchange information on the whereabouts of graves presumed to belong to missing persons, and expedite the return of remains to relatives.

Theodossiou said any process of opening up graves must be the result of thorough research, and relatives must be kept informed of inquiries and disintenment should follow internationally accepted rules as regards identification.

The Greek Cypriot side says 1,619 Greek Cypriots are missing since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded and occupied the northern third of Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
Turkish Cypriots say 803 of their community are missing from intercommunal clashes dating back to the 1960s.

"I don't want to have the same fate as my father. We don't trust the Greeks and Greek Cypriots. We don't want bones. Can they give us our father back?" said Huseyin Herguner, a 35-year-old technician.
His father, Ahmet Cemal Herguner, went missing in 1974, taken away by Greeks between the first and second operations by Turkish mainland troops.

The agreement, announced on Thursday night, is a major breakthrough in the issue which has plagued the divided Mediterranean island for decades, and one which is still considered a major stumbling block in efforts to resolve the protracted Cyprus dispute.

"I was stunned, this is is the most significant breakthrough in the issue of missing persons since 1974. I hope it leads to breakthrough on other issues as well," a senior Cypriot official told Reuters.
The decision was taken in the second meeting this week between Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides, as Greek Cypriot leader, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash in Nicosia.

Under terms of the agreement the two leaders will each designate a person, who by the end of September will exchange information on missing persons and prepare the necessary arrangements leading to the return of remains. The remains of persons known to have been killed in action on either side will also be returned to their families.
No indication has been given as to how many people may be in these graves.

"Each case will be examined on its own. If there are indications they are dead and buried the grave will be found and DNA testing will be carried out for identification purposes," said Takis Christopoulos, Presidential Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs.
Christopoulos told Reuters that a DNA bank currently in the making has gathered some 600 specimens from relatives of missing, and by September the work will be almost complete.
A tripartite committee working under U.N. auspices from the early 1980s has failed to provide conclusive evidence on the fate of any missing person.
Both leaders requested the U.N. Secretary-General to appoint a new third member to expedite the work of the committee. The position has been vacant for months.
